The Lincoln Highway, officially dedicated on October 31 1913, was one of the nation’s first coast‑to‑coast automobile routes. Conceived in 1912 by Indiana entrepreneur Carl G. Fisher, the road began at Times Square in New York City and extended westward until it terminated at Lincoln Park in San Francisco. At its inception the route traversed thirteen states—New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, Nevada, and California—before later realignments added West Virginia, bringing the total to fourteen states, 128 counties, and more than 700 municipalities that the highway passed through at various times.

Scholars can narrow the earliest performance of The Taming of the Shrew by comparing it with other works of the period. This overlap indicates that The Shrew must already have been in circulation on the stage prior to June 1592. Further evidence comes from a stage direction in a rival “A Shrew” that mentions the actor Simon Jewell, who died on 21 August 1592, establishing an August 1592 terminus ante quem for that version, and from a 1593 publication that alludes to a kissing scene unique to Shakespeare’s play. Together, these clues confirm that the first performances of The Taming of the Shrew occurred prior to June 1592.

Shakespeare’s Sonnet 116 is famously presented as a definition of steadfast love. Others, including Carol Thomas Neely, point out that “Sonnet 116” belongs to a small cluster of verses (Sonnets 94, 116, and 129) that treat love with a detached perspective, differing from the rest of Shakespeare’s sequence. In the economic history of Greece and the Greek world, it is recorded that Athens rose to become the pre‑eminent economic power in the Greek world in the late 6th century BCE.  This ascendancy was reinforced by the discovery of several silver veins in the nearby mountains, which greatly increased the city’s wealth.  Athens then organized an effective trade network with other Greek poleis, exporting large quantities of pottery and cooking vessels (archaeologists have recovered more than 80,000 amphorae and similar items in the vicinity of the city).  Although marble and bronze artworks were also traded, those luxury goods only expanded dramatically after the later Roman influence.  Because of its poor local soil, Athens eventually began importing grain to sustain its population.

Around the late 6th century BCE, Athens rose to become the pre‑eminent economic power among the Greek city‑states. This ascendancy was reinforced by the discovery of several silver veins in the nearby mountains, which greatly increased the city’s wealth. The Athenians organized an efficient trade network with other poleis, exporting large quantities of pottery and cooking vessels—over 80,000 amphorae have been recovered in excavations around the city. Although marble and bronze artworks were also traded, those luxury items only expanded dramatically after the later Roman influence. Because of its poor soil, Athens began importing grain to sustain its population.

Athens rose to become the wealthiest Greek city‑state in the late 6th century BCE, a status that was reinforced by the discovery of several silver veins in the nearby mountains. Although marble and bronze artworks were also traded, those luxury items only saw a dramatic increase after the Roman Republic’s expansion, when Greek artistic styles heavily influenced Roman culture. Because its local soil was poor, Athens eventually began importing grain to sustain its growing population.

The Christmas carol “What Child Is This?” features lyrics that were penned by William Chatterton Dix in 1865. At the time he wrote the words, Dix was employed as a manager for an insurance company and was recovering from a serious illness that sparked a spiritual renewal, prompting him to compose several hymns. His text for the carol was later paired with the traditional English folk melody “Greensleeves.” Although the piece originated in Great Britain, it has become more widely known in the United States than in its country of origin.
